beats.narration_text: Ninety-six percent. That's how often Lemonade's claims bot takes a claim straight from a customer — no human in the loop at all. And fifty-five percent of the time, it just... closes it. End to end, while you're still holding your phone. I read that in their 10-K and thought, okay — that's genuinely impressive. So how does it work? And that's the thing. They'll tell you what it achieves in detail. How it decides? Almost nothing.

stats.label: of first notice of loss, taken with no human in the loop
of claims closed end to end — instantly

props.rightNote: No dollar threshold, claim-type list or confidence score appears in any filing, letter, deck or interview.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Tanmay Kulkarni. This week I wrote a case study on Lemonade's claims automation, then built a working reference implementation of the workflow behind it — so I could see where the hard parts actually live. Three stages. Intake, Verification, Authorization Gate. A claim moves through them in order, and it stops the moment one of them says no.

props.title: Three stages
props.subtitle: A claim moves through them in order — and stops the moment one says no.

stages.name: Gate
stages.sub: settle, or hand to a human

props.escalateBody: ESCALATED → a human claims expert, assigned by specialty, qualifications, workload and schedule.

beats.narration_text: Before we open any of it up — here's what I'm going to ask at every single stage. Four questions. What's mocked? What did I make up, and does the code admit it? What happens when it says no? And could you prove, afterwards, what happened and why? That's the whole method. Watch me run it three times, then run it on your own thing.

props.title: Four questions
props.subtitle: Asked at every stage — before we open any of them.

items.label: Invented values
items.sub: What did I make up — and does the code admit it?

items.label: Failure paths
items.sub: What happens when it says no?

items.label: Accountability
items.sub: Could you prove, afterwards, what happened and why?

beats.narration_text: Let's make that concrete. The case study walks through an illustrative scenario — a customer we'll call Sofia. She isn't a real Lemonade customer; she's a worked example, deliberately built to stay inside what Lemonade has actually confirmed. So, Sofia files a claim: her dog had a vet visit for kennel cough. A hundred and twenty dollars, first of May. That's free text. Intake's whole job is turning it into something checkable — diagnosis, amount, date, and a confidence score. Point nine five here. Comfortably above threshold, so it moves on.

props.title: Intake
props.subtitle: Free text in. A checkable claim out.
props.panelNote: Escalates before any record is checked.
props.footerNote: Illustrative scenario from the case study — not a real customer

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually holding that up. In my scaffold, Intake talks to a fake adapter — deterministic, free, returns perfect JSON every single time. A real model won't. It'll wrap the JSON in an explanation, invent a field, or just time out. So you need retries with backoff, schema validation on every response, and a fallback for when it fails anyway. And it stops being free. Every claim is now a token bill and a latency budget you're answerable for.

props.title: Intake
props.subtitle: The fake adapter always answers. A real model won’t.
props.failureTitle: What a real model actually does
props.carryBody: Every claim is now a token bill and a latency budget.

beats.narration_text: Stage two. Verification runs four checks, in order, and bails at the first one that fails. Are the diagnosis, amount and date all actually there? Does a policy record exist for this customer? Is there a fraud signal on them? And does what they claimed match what the record says, within tolerance? Sofia clears all four. And notice — every rejection gets a named reason. Not "needs review." No record found. Mismatch. Fraud flag. You always know why a claim stopped.

props.title: Verification
props.subtitle: Four checks, in order. Stops at the first one that fails.
props.footerNote: Illustrative scenario from the case study — not a real customer

beats.narration_text: Both of those data sources are mocks. A fake database, a fake fraud signal. Swapping in the real ones is the easy part — as long as the interface stays identical. That's the whole reason they're separate files. The part I'd flag: keep fraud genuinely independent. Don't fold it into the record lookup as one more field. Lemonade's fraud system and its claims bot are two different things, and outside coverage keeps merging them into one — I didn't want my own code repeating that mistake. And that matching tolerance? I made it up. It's labelled, but it still needs tuning against real claims.

props.title: Verification
props.subtitle: The checks don’t change. What sits behind them does.

swaps.note: Keep it independent — never a field on the record.

props.sourceNote: Forensic Graph and AI Jim are separate systems in Lemonade’s FY2025 Form 10-K — case study §6.5.

beats.narration_text: Quick one before we go on. Two undisclosed values so far — and I invented a number for both, and labelled both. There's a third. So: what did I put in the authorization gate? Commit to an answer.

props.question: What did I put in the authorization gate?

beats.narration_text: Stage three. And this is the one I keep thinking about. Lemonade's own 10-K says AI Jim triages claims he's not authorized to settle to a human expert. So the authority has a boundary — they say so themselves. But nowhere, in any filing, shareholder letter, deck or interview, do they say where that boundary actually is. No dollar amount. No claim type. No confidence score. So — here's my authorization gate. That's the whole file. There's no rule in it at all. It calls a policy function that you have to supply. I could've put a number in there. But settlement authority might not even be a dollar amount. Writing "under five hundred" would quietly claim that it is, and I don't know that. The absence is the honest answer.

props.title: Authorization Gate
props.subtitle: The one file with no rule in it.

lines.t: """Decides whether a verified claim settles or escalates."""

props.caption: The module docstring is condensed to one line here for legibility. No logic is omitted — this is the entire file.
props.sideQuote: “…triages and assigns claims he is not authorized to settle…”
props.sideNote: The boundary is confirmed to exist. Where it sits has never been disclosed.

beats.narration_text: Which raises an obvious problem. If the gate has no rule, how does the demo run at all? It supplies one — amount under five hundred. And here's the bit I want you to notice: that number is invented, exactly like the other two. But it deliberately carries no DEV marker. Because a DEV marker is a promise — it says this is a real default, go tune it. This isn't that. It's a test prop. Labelling it would've been its own kind of lie, just a quieter one.

props.title: One invented value, unlabelled
props.subtitle: So how does the demo run at all?

lines.t: #  ^ no [DEV] marker anywhere on this line —

props.caption: Both are invented numbers. Only two of them claim to be defaults.
props.sideQuote: A [DEV] marker is a promise: “this is a real default — go tune it.”
props.sideSource: DESIGN_DECISIONS.md, Decision 2 — a named, logged exception.
props.sideNote: The demo policy isn’t a default. It’s a test prop. Labelling it would have been its own kind of lie.

beats.narration_text: Which makes this the stage that production changes most. Because in a real insurer, that policy function isn't code somebody writes on a Tuesday. It's a decision a compliance team signs off on. So you'd need an audit trail — every claim, the inputs, the outcome, and which version of the policy decided it. You'd need to explain a denial to a regulator in plain English. You'd need idempotency, so a retry never pays the same claim twice. None of that is in my scaffold. All of it is non-negotiable in production.

props.title: Authorization Gate
props.subtitle: The file stays empty. Everything around it doesn’t.

layers.title: Audit record
layers.sub: every claim, its inputs, its outcome

layers.title: Explanation
layers.sub: why, in language a regulator accepts

layers.title: Idempotency
layers.sub: a retry never pays the same claim twice

props.coreSub: no rule · no default · no [DEV] marker
props.carryLabel: None of this is in the scaffold
props.carryBody: All of it is non-negotiable before a real claim reaches it.

beats.narration_text: Forty-three tests, all green — and here's what that buys you. The wiring is proven. Some of these use spies to show a rejected claim never even reaches the next stage — not that it returned the right answer, that the later code never ran. So you don't have to build any of that. Clone it, add your API key, and you're straight into the interesting part: watching a real model hit these stages, and finding where your own claim data breaks it. That's the one thing tests can't tell you. Everything else is done.

props.title: 43 passing
props.subtitle: What that actually buys you.
props.caption: Real output, 2026-08-10. Per-claim text lines omitted for legibility; outcomes verbatim.
props.sideQuote: The structure is proven. Clone it, add your key, and the same pipeline runs on a real model.
props.sideSource: export LLM_PROVIDER=claude  ·  export LLM_API_KEY=…   — that’s the entire change.
props.sideNote: The one thing tests can’t tell you: how a real model behaves on your own claim data. That’s the part worth your time.

beats.narration_text: So — your turn. Take something you've built that talks to a model. A demo, a prototype, anything. And run those same four questions on it. What's mocked. What you invented, and whether the code says so. What happens when it refuses. And whether you could prove, afterwards, what it did. Write the answers down, then pick the single one that'd break first with real users on it. That's not a to-do list — it's your honest distance from production. And you'll be closer than you think on most of it. You'll just know exactly where you're not.

props.command: For each stage of my pipeline: what's mocked, what did I invent, what happens on failure, and could I prove what happened?
output: 2 · Invented values — does the code admit it?
3 · Failure paths — what happens when it says no?
4 · Accountability — could you prove what happened?
Then: which one breaks first with real users on it?
